MUQATIL:2:268/r1.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:268/r1.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:268/r1.claim: Satan threatens poverty when people give charity and commands them to withhold it; Muqatil glosses the command to indecency as withholding charity.

MUQATIL:2:268/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:268/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:268/r2.claim: God promises forgiveness for sins and replacement of charity in worldly life, as well as forgiveness in the hereafter.

MUQATIL:2:268/r3.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:268/r3.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:268/r3.claim: The promise to lend God a goodly loan means giving sincere, willing charity, which God multiplies in this life and forgives in the next.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p109#3/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p109#3/r1.speaker: عبيد الله بن عبد الله بن مسعود
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p109#3/r1.claim: A person receives an angelic prompting toward good and truth, for which he should praise God, or a satanic prompting toward evil and denial of truth, from which he should seek refuge.

AKHFASH:v1p200/r2.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p200/r2.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p200/r2.claim: Some compare الفقر with the two forms of الضعف and analyze يعد as taking two objects.

TUSTARI:2:268/r1.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:2:268/r1.speaker: author
TUSTARI:2:268/r1.claim: Satan’s promise of poverty and command to indecency mean taking something unlawfully and putting it where it does not belong.

TAB-FULL:v5p5/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v5p5/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v5p5/r1.claim: Satan threatens poverty to deter obligatory charity and urges disobedience, while God promises forgiveness through charity and replenishment with increased provision.

TAB-FULL:v5p5/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v5p5/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v5p5/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās divides the promises: Satan says to withhold wealth for future need, while God promises forgiveness and increased provision.

TAB-FULL:v5p5/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v5p5/r3.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v5p5/r3.claim: Qatāda glosses God's promise as forgiveness for sins and bounty in place of poverty.

TAB-FULL:v5p5/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v5p5/r4.speaker: النبي
TAB-FULL:v5p5/r4.claim: The Prophet describes an angelic prompting toward good and truth and a satanic prompting toward evil and denial of truth; respond with praise or refuge accordingly.

TAB-FULL:v5p5/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v5p5/r5.speaker: عبد الله
TAB-FULL:v5p5/r5.claim: ʿAbd Allāh repeats that an angel's prompting encourages good and truth, while Satan's encourages evil, and advises seeking refuge or forgiveness.

TAB-FULL:v5p8/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v5p8/r1.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
TAB-FULL:v5p8/r1.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reports that the angel prompts good and truth and Satan prompts evil and denial; praise God for the former and seek refuge from the latter.

ZAJJAJ:v1p350/r5.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p350/r5.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p350/r5.claim: Both faqr and fuqr are used for poverty; Satan’s threat is that giving good goods will make people poor, with the preposition bi omitted after yaʿid.

ZAJJAJ:v1p350/r6.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p350/r6.speaker: الشاعر
ZAJJAJ:v1p350/r6.claim: An unnamed poet’s ‘I commanded you good’ illustrates direct transitive use of a verb that normally takes bi.

ZAJJAJ:v1p350/r7.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p350/r7.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p350/r7.claim: The verb waʿada has several verbal-noun forms, including waʿd, ʿida, mawʿid, mawʿida, mawʿūd, and mawʿūda.

ZAJJAJ:v1p350/r8.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p350/r8.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p350/r8.claim: Al-faḥshāʾ here means failing to give charity and thereby severing social ties.

ZAJJAJ:v1p350/r9.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p350/r9.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p350/r9.claim: God promises forgiveness for charity and to replace what donors spend; He gives from abundance and knows where to place it, including the unseen and visible.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p529#2/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p529#2/r2.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNABIHATIM:v2p529#2/r2.claim: The Prophet says Satanic prompting urges evil and denies truth, while angelic prompting urges good and confirms truth; praise God for the latter and seek refuge for the former.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p529#2/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p529#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v2p529#2/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says two clauses are from God and two from Satan; Satan promises poverty and urges people to hold onto money for future need.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p529#2/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p529#2/r4.speaker: منصور
IBNABIHATIM:v2p529#2/r4.claim: Mansur interprets Satan's promise of poverty as long-range wishful thinking.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p529#2/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p529#2/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v2p529#2/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses the command to commit obscenity as a command to do evil.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p529#2/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p529#2/r6.speaker: مقاتل بن حيان
IBNABIHATIM:v2p529#2/r6.claim: Muqatil says obscenity means sins, and the source says Sa'id ibn Jubayr reported the same gloss.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p529#2/r7.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p529#2/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v2p529#2/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the obscenity as adultery; the same interpretation is also reported from Hasan, Ikrima, and al-Suddi.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p529#2/r8.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p529#2/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v2p529#2/r8.claim: Ibn Abbas says God promises forgiveness for these sins.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p529#2/r9.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p529#2/r9.speaker: قتادة
IBNABIHATIM:v2p529#2/r9.claim: Qatada says God promises forgiveness for people's sins; Ibn al-Mubarak explains obscenities here as sins.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p531/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p531/r1.speaker: مقاتل بن حيان
IBNABIHATIM:v2p531/r1.claim: Muqatil says God promises to forgive people's sins when they give charity.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p531/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p531/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v2p531/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets God's promised bounty as provision.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p531/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p531/r3.speaker: قتادة
IBNABIHATIM:v2p531/r3.claim: Qatada says God's bounty will relieve people's poverty.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p531/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p531/r4.speaker: مقاتل بن حيان
IBNABIHATIM:v2p531/r4.claim: Muqatil says God will replace what people spend.

NAHHAS:v1p335/r3.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p335/r3.speaker: سيبويه
NAHHAS:v1p335/r3.claim: يأمركم takes two objects; non-Qur'anic usage may omit bā' in يأمركم الفحشاء, as Sibawayh's verse shows.

SULAMI:v1p80#3/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p80#3/r1.speaker: author
SULAMI:v1p80#3/r1.claim: Satan's promise of poverty means greed and miserliness, while God directs people to contentment, spending, and generosity, promising forgiveness and bounty.

SULAMI:v1p80#3/r2.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p80#3/r2.speaker: محمد بن الفضل
SULAMI:v1p80#3/r2.claim: Satan says generosity will impoverish you and commands miserliness; God promises forgiveness and bounty for generosity.

SULAMI:v1p80#3/r3.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p80#3/r3.speaker: أبو عثمان
SULAMI:v1p80#3/r3.claim: Satan threatens poverty if one abandons worldly life, while God promises forgiveness and bounty for turning away from it.

SULAMI:v1p80#3/r4.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p80#3/r4.speaker: محمد بن علي
SULAMI:v1p80#3/r4.claim: Satan calls generosity poverty and commands miserliness, which builds his house; God promises forgiveness for building the homecoming and sufficiency in Him alone.

SULAMI:v1p80#3/r5.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p80#3/r5.speaker: أبو بكر الوراق
SULAMI:v1p80#3/r5.claim: The servant should counter Satan's threat by openly recalling God's favors and blessings upon him.

THALABI:v2p270/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p270/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p270/r1.claim: In “Satan promises you poverty,” the preposition bi is understood but omitted; a line of poetry illustrates the construction.

THALABI:v2p270/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p270/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p270/r2.claim: Arabic commonly uses waʿada for a promise of good and awʿada for a threat of harm, though either verb can occur with either object; the source cites Qurʾan and poetry.

THALABI:v2p270/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p270/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p270/r3.claim: Poverty means bad circumstances and lack of means; its two vowelings are like the two forms of ḍaʿf. The word is associated with a broken vertebra.

THALABI:v2p270/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p270/r4.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p270/r4.claim: Satan frightens a person that charity will impoverish him and urges him to hold his wealth back; fahshāʾ here means miserliness and withholding zakat.

THALABI:v2p270/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p270/r5.speaker: مقاتل بن حيان
THALABI:v2p270/r5.claim: Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān says every Qurʾanic use of fahshāʾ means fornication except this verse.

THALABI:v2p270/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p270/r6.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p270/r6.claim: God's promise means recompense: God's promise comes through inspiration and revelation, while Satan's consists of whispers and imaginings.

THALABI:v2p270/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p270/r7.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p270/r7.claim: God promises forgiveness for sins and bounty in the form of provision and replacement; a Torah saying is cited about spending from God's provision to receive His favor.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p343/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p343/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p343/r1.claim: Satan's promise of poverty is his warning that spending or giving charity will make a person poor.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p343/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p343/r2.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p343/r2.claim: Satan's command to indecency may mean stinginess or sins.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p343/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p343/r3.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p343/r3.claim: God's promise of forgiveness includes pardon; the passage's first stated explanation is damaged and incomplete.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p343/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p343/r4.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p343/r4.claim: God's promise of fadl may mean abundant provision or doubled punishment.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p343/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p343/r5.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p343/r5.claim: The Prophet describes Satan's prompting as a promise of evil and denial of truth, and the angel's as a promise of good and affirmation of truth; respond to the former by seeking refuge and praise God for the latter.

QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r10.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r10.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r10.claim: Other forms of the threat attach the heart to needless things and obscure the perception of God’s sufficiency.

QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r11.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r11.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r11.claim: Satan’s command to indecency means craving worldly life and the means that intensify greed, hope, and forgetfulness of contentment.

QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r12.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r12.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r12.claim: Indecency also includes following appetites, preferring personal interests, looking toward others, or allowing anything besides God into the mind.

QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r13.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r13.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r13.claim: Indecency includes retreating to easy rationalizations after truth is clear and returning to what one left for God.

QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r14.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r14.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r14.claim: The promised bounty is contentment in this life and reward, gardens, vision, and divine pleasure in the next.

QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r15.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r15.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r15.claim: Its immediate spiritual gifts include victory over the self, the opening of gnosis, nearness, and intimate disclosures.

QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r7.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r7.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r7.claim: Satan promises poverty while God promises forgiveness and bounty.

QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r8.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r8.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r8.claim: Satan’s poverty threat urges people to hoard what they know and cultivate greed through his obedience.

QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r9.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r9.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r9.claim: Satan also threatens poverty by making people rely on their own planning and forget God’s accustomed generosity.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p428/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p428/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p428/r1.claim: Both فقر and فقر are dialect forms for poverty or weakness caused by limited possessions; the root means a broken vertebra, and the source cites Tarafa and Labid.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p428/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p428/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p428/r2.claim: For poverty opposite wealth, no فَعَلَ verb is attested; instead God makes someone poor and he becomes poor.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p428/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p428/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p428/r3.claim: Satan threatens people with poverty, telling them to keep their wealth because giving charity will make them poor.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p428/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p428/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p428/r4.claim: Fahshāʾ here means miserliness and withholding zakat; Muqatil and al-Kalbi say elsewhere in the Qur'an it means fornication.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p428/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p428/r5.speaker: مقاتل والكلبي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p428/r5.claim: They say every Qur'anic occurrence of فحشاء means fornication except this verse, where it means miserliness.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p428/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p428/r6.speaker: الأزهري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p428/r6.claim: Arabs call a miser فاحش; he cites Tarafa's verse describing the miser who hoards wealth.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p430/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p430/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p430/r1.claim: God promises to reward charity by forgiving sins and replacing what was spent.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:268-269/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:268-269/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:268-269/r1.claim: Satan frightens people with poverty and tells them to keep their money, since giving charity would impoverish them.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:268-269/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:268-269/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:268-269/r2.claim: The indecency Satan commands is miserliness, including withholding zakat; God promises forgiveness and compensation for charity.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p333/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p333/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p333/r1.claim: The devil promises poverty by frightening people that charity will leave them poor; poverty means bad circumstances and little property, and its root evokes a broken vertebra.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p333/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p333/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p333/r2.claim: The wording distinguishes promising good from threatening evil when the object is unspoken; the author illustrates it with verses about promised spoils and the Fire.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p333/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p333/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p333/r3.claim: Here indecency means miserliness and withholding zakat; al-Kalbi says indecency elsewhere in the Qur'an means adultery, except in this verse.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p333/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p333/r4.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p333/r4.claim: God promises forgiveness of sins and replacement provision; He is abundant in wealth and knowledge.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p333/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p333/r5.speaker: أبو هريرة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p333/r5.claim: Abu Hurayra reports God's promise, 'Spend, son of Adam, and I will spend on you'; the Prophet says God's giving never diminishes despite continuous spending since creation.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p333/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p333/r6.speaker: أسماء
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p333/r6.claim: The Prophet told Asma to give without counting or hoarding, lest God withhold from her.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p343/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p343/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p343/r1.claim: In the context of spending, Satan predicts that giving will leave people poor.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p343/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p343/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p343/r2.claim: The word poverty has readings with a damma or two fathas.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p343/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p343/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p343/r3.claim: A promise can concern either good or evil, as the Qur'an also says of Hell.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p343/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p343/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p343/r4.claim: Satan commands miserliness and withholding charity; Arabs call a miser fāḥish.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p343/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p343/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p343/r5.claim: God promises forgiveness and expiation, plus replacement better than the gift or a reward in the afterlife.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363#2/r1.claim: These verses draw people toward charity by exposing Satan's whispering and hostility, recalling God's reward and gift of wisdom, and urging reflection on spending and vows, whether public or hidden.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363#2/r2.claim: An unrestricted promise normally denotes good, but here the promise is explicitly attached to the unwelcome prospect of poverty; fahshāʾ covers all ugly acts and all sins.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363#2/r3.speaker: حيوة عن رجل من أهل الرباط
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363#2/r3.claim: A man from the border garrisons recited al-faqr with ḍamma on the fāʾ, a dialectal form.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363#2/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363#2/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas says the verse contains two prompts from Satan and two from God.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363#2/r5.speaker: ابن مسعود، النبي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363#2/r5.claim: The Prophet reports that Satan's prompting threatens evil and denies truth, while the angel's prompting promises truth and confirms good; he recited this verse and advised seeking refuge from Satan's prompting.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363#2/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363#2/r6.claim: Forgiveness means God's covering of servants in this world and the next; فضل means provision and expansion in this world and bliss in the next, all of which God promises.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363#2/r7.speaker: النقاش
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363#2/r7.claim: Al-Naqqash notes an argument that poverty is preferable to wealth because Satan deters people from good by frightening them with poverty.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363#2/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363#2/r8.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363#2/r8.claim: The verse is not decisive proof that poverty is superior, although the counterargument is forceful.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363#2/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363#2/r9.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363#2/r9.claim: A Torah report promises that spending from God's provision will bring expanded bounty, and Qur'an 34:39 confirms it.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p364/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p364/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p364/r1.claim: God is واسع because His mercy and knowledge encompass everything.

TABRISI:2:268/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:268/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:268/r1.claim: Faqr means need, opposite of wealth; related forms describe poverty, the back vertebrae, a calamity that breaks them, and a mount lowered for riding.

TABRISI:2:268/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:268/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:268/r2.claim: Waʿd, promise, can refer to good or evil when qualified, but when unqualified or left vague it denotes good; waʿīd is specifically a threat of evil.

TABRISI:2:268/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:268/r3.speaker: علي بن عيسى
TABRISI:2:268/r3.claim: ʿAlī b. ʿĪsā glosses faḥshāʾ as sins; the miser is called fāḥish because refusing guests and petitioners is offensive, as illustrated by poetry of Ṭarafa and Kaʿb.

TABRISI:2:268/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:268/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:268/r4.claim: Satan frightens people that giving to good causes or giving their best wealth will make them poor; one view specifies payment of zakat.

TABRISI:2:268/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:268/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:268/r5.claim: Satan's command to faḥshāʾ means sins and abandoning obedience, or spending from inferior wealth; that is disobedience and can sever ties when the wealthy withhold from needy kin and neighbors.

TABRISI:2:268/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:268/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:268/r6.claim: God promises that giving the best wealth will cover sins and pardon punishment, replace the gift with better provision, and increase His bounty.

TABRISI:2:268/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:268/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:2:268/r7.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās divides the promises into two from God—pardon and increased provision—and two from Satan—fear of poverty and an order to sin.

TABRISI:2:268/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:268/r8.speaker: ابن مسعود
TABRISI:2:268/r8.claim: Ibn Masʿūd, with a similar report from Abū ʿAbd Allāh, describes one prompting from Satan and one from the angel: Satan urges poverty and sin, while the angel urges giving and forbids sin.

TABRISI:2:268/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:268/r9.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:268/r9.claim: God's breadth means that giving does not harm Him or diminish His stores; He knows who deserves a gift.

RAZI-FULL:v7p56#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p56#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p56#2/r1.claim: The Satan who promises poverty may be Iblīs, all devils, devils among jinn and humans, or the lower self commanding evil.

RAZI-FULL:v7p56#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p56#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p56#2/r2.claim: Promise can describe good or evil; calling punishment a promise may be ironic, like announcing painful punishment as glad tidings.

RAZI-FULL:v7p56#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p56#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p56#2/r3.claim: Faqr and faqr are two forms for poverty; its root is breaking the backbone, illustrated by Ṭarafa's line, and al-Kashshāf notes two vocalized readings.

RAZI-FULL:v7p56#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p56#2/r4.speaker: ابن مسعود
RAZI-FULL:v7p56#2/r4.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reports that Satan whispers an evil promise while an angel whispers good; the hearer should recognize the source, seek God's protection, and he recited this verse.

RAZI-FULL:v7p56#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p56#2/r5.speaker: الحسن
RAZI-FULL:v7p56#2/r5.claim: Al-Ḥasan transmits an emigrant's advice: a person can locate Satan's influence by noticing where he feels an urge to do wrong.

RAZI-FULL:v7p56#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p56#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p56#2/r6.claim: One interpretation of الفحشاء is miserliness: Satan first frightens people with poverty because stinginess is universally despised, then urges them to withhold charity and obligations; Ṭarafa's verse uses فاحش for miser.

RAZI-FULL:v7p57/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p57/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p57/r1.claim: A second reading of الفحشاء is escalation into all wrongdoing: fear of poverty first stops quality giving, then all charity and obligatory duties, numbing conscience until further sins become easy.

RAZI-FULL:v7p57/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p57/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p57/r2.claim: Generosity is the virtuous extreme of giving all; refusing all is the deficient extreme, while withholding quality goods but giving poor goods is the middle step by which Satan draws a person toward total refusal.

RAZI-FULL:v7p57/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p57/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p57/r3.claim: A report from the Prophet says an angel calls each night for God to replace the spender's wealth and bring loss to the person who hoards it.

RAZI-FULL:v7p57/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p57/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p57/r4.claim: The hereafter's promise deserves trust over Satan's worldly poverty threat: the afterlife is certain, God's forgiveness is guaranteed, hoarded wealth may be unusable, worldly pleasure ends, and afterlife benefits are lasting and pure.

RAZI-FULL:v7p58/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p58/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p58/r1.claim: مغفرة means erasure of sins, as in Q 9:103; its indefinite form and the phrase منه magnify it because the giver's greatness magnifies the gift.

RAZI-FULL:v7p58/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p58/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p58/r2.claim: The exceptional forgiveness may turn sins into good deeds, make the donor an intercessor for other sinners, or include afterlife realities beyond present human understanding.

RAZI-FULL:v7p58/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p58/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p58/r3.claim: فضل can mean worldly recompense, but al-Rāzī prefers social goodwill: people helped by a generous person pray for and assist him, opening worldly good; he also explains psychological and spiritual benefits of giving.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:268#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:268#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:2:268#2/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas cites the promise that whatever people spend God replaces, and that He is the best provider; the author adds that 'vast, knowing' describes generous giving and knowledge of its proper recipients and all things.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:268#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:268#2/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:268#2/r2.claim: God's being vast and knowing means He gives from abundance, knows where to place His gift, and knows both the unseen and seen.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r1.claim: Satan's promise means frightening people with poverty so they will not spend; the verse follows the charity teaching because Satan discourages spending for God and urges sins, including spending on sins.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r10.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r10.claim: A Torah saying promises expanded favor to the servant who spends from God's provision, and Ibn Abbas cites 34:39 as its Qur'anic confirmation: God replaces what is spent and is the best provider.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r2.claim: Another interpretation is that Satan urges people not to give, leading them to disobedience and severed kinship.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r3.claim: The word faqr is also read with a ḍamma on the first letter, like the dialectal variants for weakness.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r4.claim: In ordinary Arabic, an unqualified promise concerns good; when the promised content is specified, it can refer to good or evil, and this verse uses promise in both senses.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas says the verse contains two promises from God and two from Satan.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r6.speaker: رسول الله
QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r6.claim: Ibn Masud reports the Prophet's distinction between Satan's prompt, which threatens evil and denies truth, and the angel's prompt, which promises good and affirms truth; al-Tirmidhi grades the hadith hasan sahih.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r7.speaker: سيبويه
QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r7.claim: Outside Qur'anic recitation, one can say 'command you evil' without the preposition bā; Sibawayh cites a poem with the same construction.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r8.claim: Maghfira is God's covering of people in this world and the next; faḍl is provision and expansion in this world and bliss in the next.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r9.speaker: النقاش
QURTUBI-FULL:2:268/r9.claim: Al-Naqqash notes that some infer poverty is better than wealth because Satan's fear of poverty turns people away from good; Ibn Atiyya says this is not decisive and has a strong counterargument.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:268/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:268/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:268/r1.claim: Satan promises poverty to discourage spending; the noun is read with several combinations of vowel length and case.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:268/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:268/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:268/r2.claim: Fahsha may mean miserliness, since Arabs call a miser indecent, or sins more generally.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:268/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:268/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:268/r3.claim: God promises forgiveness for sins to those who spend, and increased provision either in this world or the next.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:268/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:268/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:268/r4.claim: God is abundant in bounty toward the spender and knows the spending.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p131#2/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p131#2/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p131#2/r1.claim: Satan promises that spending will make people poor; the word promise can refer to either good or evil.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p131#2/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p131#2/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p131#2/r2.claim: Satan's command to indecency means inciting miserliness and withholding charity; Arabs call a miser fāḥish.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p131#2/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p131#2/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p131#2/r3.claim: God promises forgiveness and expiation for sins, plus either better replacement for what was spent or reward in the afterlife.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p131#2/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p131#2/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p131#2/r4.claim: God grants expansively to whom He wills and knows people's actions and intentions.

QASHANI:2:268/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:268/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:268/r1.claim: Satan promises poverty and urges miserliness, the ugly trait, so seekers should seek God's protection.

QASHANI:2:268/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:268/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:268/r2.claim: God promises to veil the ego's qualities with His light and grant gifts from His attributes, such as absolute richness, removing fear of poverty.

QASHANI:2:268/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:268/r3.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:268/r3.claim: God's generosity has no narrow vessel or end, and He knows where manifestations can occur and each recipient's readiness and merit.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p682/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p682/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p682/r1.claim: The cited poem shows fahshāʾ can mean obscene speech.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p682/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p682/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p682/r2.claim: The poem says the group avoids obscene speech both among its own people and outsiders.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p682/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p682/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p682/r3.claim: If someone refuses to give, Satan may then urge him to answer the petitioner rudely and overwhelm him with insulting words.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p682/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p682/r4.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p682/r4.claim: He reports the Prophet describing satanic promptings as promises of evil and denial of truth, and angelic promptings as promises of truth and affirmation of good; the listener should seek refuge or praise God, and the Prophet recited this verse.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p682/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p682/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p682/r5.claim: The promise comes before the command because it first makes the listener feel secure with Satan; once fear of poverty takes hold, Satan commands him.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p682/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p682/r6.speaker: الزمخشري وأبو مسلم
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p682/r6.claim: They take الفاحش as a miser and fahshāʾ as miserliness and withholding charity; al-Zamakhshari sees the second clause as reinforcing the first.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p682/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p682/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p682/r7.claim: He disputes that the cited poetry proves الفاحش means miserly: the usages can mean bad character, ugliness, or rude treatment, with stinginess inferred from refusing food.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p683/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p683/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p683/r1.claim: God promises forgiveness as covering sins in return for giving and فضل as an increase beyond the due reward; other views take the increase as replacement wealth or afterlife reward.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p683/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p683/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p683/r2.claim: The promises counter the satanic motive behind giving inferior goods: God promises both covering sins and increased provision or reward in this life and the next.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p683/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p683/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p683/r3.claim: A Torah report says God will expand favor for a servant who spends from God's provision; the Qur'an affirms the promise that God replaces what people spend.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p683/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p683/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p683/r4.claim: Wāsiʿ means generous in bounty, and ʿalīm means knowing spenders' intentions or where to place His favor.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p683/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p683/r5.speaker: البراء
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p683/r5.claim: He reports the Prophet saying God loves spending and dislikes stinginess, and urges people to eat and feed without hoarding.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p683/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p683/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p683/r6.claim: The Prophet also called miserliness an especially bad disease.

SAMIN-DURR:2:268/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:268/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:268/r1.claim: الشيطان يعدكم is a subject-predicate sentence; وعد drops its root wāw in يعِدكم between yāʾ and kasra.

SAMIN-DURR:2:268/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:268/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:268/r2.claim: Most read الفقر with fatḥa and still qāf; Abū Ḥaywa reports a ḍamma form, and another reading has both vowels open.

SAMIN-DURR:2:268/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:268/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:268/r3.claim: منه may qualify مغفرة through an omitted phrase, or be the object of يعد, meaning ‘promises you from himself’; in the first analysis فضلا also omits منه.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p699/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p699/r3.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p699/r3.claim: Ibn Masud reports that Satan whispers evil and denial of truth, while the angel whispers good and confirms truth; the person should praise God for the good impulse and seek refuge for the other.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p699/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p699/r4.speaker: الترمذي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p699/r4.claim: Al-Tirmidhi grades the raised Ibn Masud report hasan gharib and says Abu al-Ahwas is its only known transmitter in this marfu form.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p700/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p700/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p700/r1.claim: A route through Musar makes the lamma report Ibn Masud’s own statement rather than a Prophetic report; Ibn Kathir leaves the matter to God.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p700/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p700/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p700/r2.claim: Satan frightens people with poverty so they withhold charity, then urges sins and forbidden acts; God instead promises forgiveness and bounty.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r12.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r12.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r12.claim: The warning about Satan counters the question why people are usually miserly after hearing God's true promise: the enemy promises the opposite and lies.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r13.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r13.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r13.claim: Satan's name evokes ruin and distance; either trait alone warrants avoiding him, and their combination makes avoidance still more urgent.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r14.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r14.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r14.claim: Fear of poverty drives worldly people to sever ties, withdraw, hoard, and remain poor; even the owner of the world is poor if greedy, while the content are rich.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r15.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r15.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r15.claim: A servant of the Rich should know he is enriched by his Master; fearing poverty is the servant's flight from his Lord, and poverty is lacking what one needs when needed.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r16.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r16.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r16.claim: Satan's command to indecency undermines charity through reminders, injury, and other appetites, potentially destroying property and lives.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r17.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r17.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r17.claim: Fahsha covers everything jointly condemned by reason, religious law, and nature; here its chief referent is miserliness, the gravest disease and root of worldly and next-worldly evil.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r18.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r18.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r18.claim: God promises forgiveness for human shortcomings and increased bounty in both worlds; every blessing is a gift of His grace.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r19.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r19.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r19.claim: Calling God expansive and knowing weakens Satan's scheme and promises the person tempted by fear of poverty and indecency that God knows human weakness and susceptibility to whispers.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r20.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r20.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r20.claim: The final parable passage closes with encouragement and warning, as the opening of the parables did.

DURR-FULL:v2p64/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p64/r3.speaker: ابن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v2p64/r3.claim: Satan whispers evil and denies truth, while the angel promises good and affirms truth; recognize the latter as from God and seek refuge from Satan for the former.

DURR-FULL:v2p64/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p64/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p64/r4.claim: Satan's promise of poverty means hoarding rather than spending; God promises forgiveness for sins and provision.

DURR-FULL:v2p64/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p64/r5.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v2p64/r5.claim: God promises forgiveness for people's obscenities and provision for their poverty.

DURR-FULL:v2p64/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p64/r6.speaker: خالد الربعي
DURR-FULL:v2p64/r6.claim: He reflects on three verses, including God's promise of forgiveness and bounty against Satan's threat of poverty; he also cites 40:60 and 2:152.

DURR-FULL:v2p64/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p64/r7.speaker: ابن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v2p64/r7.claim: A person is between God and Satan: if God has use for him, He protects him from Satan; otherwise He leaves him to Satan.

BURSEVI:v1p352/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p352/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p352/r1.claim: A promise is information about what the speaker will bring about later, and the word can describe a bad outcome as well as a good one.

BURSEVI:v1p352/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p352/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p352/r2.claim: The Qur'an calls Hell a promise to disbelievers, showing that the word applies to harm too.

BURSEVI:v1p352/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p352/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p352/r3.claim: Satan frightens people with poverty and tells them to keep their wealth lest charity make them poor.

BURSEVI:v1p352/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p352/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p352/r4.claim: Fāḥshāʾ here is stinginess and withholding charity; Arabs call a miser fāḥish.

BURSEVI:v1p352/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p352/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p352/r5.claim: God promises forgiveness and replacement greater than what was spent in this world, as well as reward in the next, refuting Satan.

BURSEVI:v1p352/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p352/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p352/r6.claim: God has ample power and bounty to fulfill His promise and knows each gift, so He does not waste its reward.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p40#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p40#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p40#2/r1.claim: The author points to a parallel verse for this divine statement about recompense.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r1.claim: The verse explains why people target inferior goods: Satan frightens donors that spending good wealth will make them poor; the threat is presented as certain, as if caused by Satan himself.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r10.claim: The second coordinated noun omits a quality recoverable from the first; God is expansive in mercy and bounty and knows what donors give to repay it.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r2.claim: Some claim the threat is actually a promise of good because poverty caused by giving is virtuous; the author says this is far from the Qur’an’s intent.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r3.claim: Faqr has several transmitted vocalizations, and its root refers to breaking the vertebrae of the back.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r4.claim: The disgraceful command is chiefly stinginess and withholding charity; Arabs called a miser fāḥish, as in Kaʿb’s verse, while broader sins or adultery are also suggested.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r5.speaker: كعب
ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r5.claim: Kaʿb’s line uses fāḥish to describe a man who is not lewd or miserly at home or in company, illustrating the word’s application to miserliness.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r6.claim: Here ‘commands’ metaphorically means incites and urges, a transferred metaphor; the warning comes first because once fear of poverty settles, Satan dominates with commands.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r7.claim: God promises forgiveness and bounty through the Prophet; forgiveness may cover sins or, according to Qatāda, the stinginess just condemned, while bounty is provision or replacement.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r8.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains bounty as provision or compensation, pairing forgiveness for the afterlife with worldly benefit; a hadith has two angels pray each morning for spenders’ replacement and misers’ loss.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p40/r9.claim: Others place both forgiveness and bounty in the afterlife, with forgiveness first because removing harm precedes granting benefit; the author links this to 3:185.

ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r14.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r14.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r14.claim: Satan may be the despairing Iblis, any devilish whisperer, or the commanding self; he frightens people with poverty and urges stinginess and spending on sins and base desires.

ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r15.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r15.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r15.claim: God promises forgiveness for sins, multiplied replacement for worldly spending, and happiness and reward in both worlds.

ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r16.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r16.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r16.claim: God's bounty is abundant and His knowledge is complete, so He knows the value of each gift, rewards it, and is not constrained in fulfilling His promise.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p59/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p59/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p59/r1.claim: The verse follows the command to give good property: Satan discourages giving the best and tempts people to hoard, donate inferior goods, or fear poverty.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p59/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p59/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p59/r2.claim: Putting Satan first signals condemnation and warning, while subject-first order also strengthens the assertion that he promises poverty.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p59/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p59/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p59/r3.claim: Satan's promise is a figurative assurance that poverty will follow spending, modeled on God's genuine promise; it reflects the certainty conveyed by a promise.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p59/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p59/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p59/r4.claim: If promise can refer to good and evil, as al-Qāmūs follows Thaʿlab's Faṣīḥ, the expression has one figure; if promise is only good, as al-Zamakhsharī says in al-Asās, it has two.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p59/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p59/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p59/r5.claim: Poverty derives from breaking the backbone, portraying incapacity; the word has several vocalizations, and فقير can function as a verbal-noun adjective.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p60/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p60/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p60/r1.claim: Faḥshāʾ names a very vile act or utterance deserving blame; it comes from exceeding limits and does not mean miserliness, though a miser can be called fāḥish. Satan's command is figurative whispering, not literal speech, and the definite article marks the class.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p60/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p60/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p60/r2.claim: God's real promise of forgiveness and bounty contrasts with Satan's temptation; placing God's name first likewise strengthens the assertion.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p60/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p60/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p60/r3.claim: Wāsiʿ means abundant in grace and giving, as in the prayer that God's mercy and knowledge encompass all things; a report describes the Prophet as expansive in warmth and character.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#8/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#8/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274#8/r3.claim: Al-Qummī explains Satan's promise as telling people not to spend because they will become poor, while God's promise is forgiveness and replacement for giving in His cause.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#8/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#8/r4.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
TABATABAI:2:261-274#8/r4.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reports the Prophet teaching that Satan's influence promises evil and denies truth, while the angel's influence promises good and confirms truth; one should thank God for the latter and seek refuge from the former. Al-Tirmidhī grades the report hasan.

TABATABAI:2:261-274/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274/r1.claim: The connected themes suggest this passage was revealed as one unit: spending grows seven hundredfold or more, sincere giving bears fruit, ostentation and reminders or harm ruin reward, good wealth should be given, the poor detained in God's path are recipients, and the reward is great.

TABATABAI:2:261-274/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274/r2.claim: The passage orders its teaching around purpose (giving for God, not people), manner (without reproach or injury), quality (good rather than bad wealth), recipient (the needy constrained in God's path), and reward.

TABATABAI:2:268-269/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:268-269/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:268-269/r1.claim: The Qur’an distinguishes truth from error: truth is from God and error is from Satan, as shown by the cited verses.

TABATABAI:2:268-269/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:268-269/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:268-269/r2.claim: The cross-referenced verses about truth and error are all Meccan.

TABATABAI:2:268-269/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:268-269/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:268-269/r3.claim: God's promise is contrasted with Satan's by setting each cause in place of its effect; the comparison asks givers to choose the promise best for them.

TABATABAI:2:268-269/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:268-269/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:268-269/r4.claim: The argument is that fear of poverty is a satanic delusion, while the forgiveness and increase promised for giving good wealth are a truthful promise from the all-knowing, all-encompassing God.

TABATABAI:2:268/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:268/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:268/r1.claim: The verse argues that choosing poor-quality goods is not good for donors, while giving good goods serves their interest; they withhold good assets because they fear reducing their wealth.

TABATABAI:2:268/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:268/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:268/r2.claim: The fear of poverty is Satan's insinuation: spending resembles a transaction that brings recompense, and God alone enriches and grants livelihood, as 53:48 says.

TABATABAI:2:268/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:268/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:268/r3.claim: By naming Satan's promise instead of the donors' fear, the verse identifies the fear as harmful; Satan leads to falsehood either directly or through something that appears true.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:268/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:268/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:268/r1.claim: God and Satan are the two sources of thoughts and feelings: God guides people toward good, while human and jinn devils try to turn them from God's path and inspire negative thoughts.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:268/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:268/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:268/r2.claim: People must follow the right guidance; those who do are the wise people discussed in the next verse.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:268/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:268/r3.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:268/r3.claim: A selfish, satanic use of reason treats aid without immediate material return as foolish, whereas wisdom sees eternal reward, the happiness charity brings, social bonds, and reduced class conflict as genuine benefit.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:268/r4.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:268/r4.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:268/r4.claim: God promises forgiveness and bounty to sincere donors and inspires wisdom; Satan instead plants miserliness, selfishness, and fear of poverty, leading to ugly and inhuman behavior.

QIRAAT-ER:2:268:5#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:2:268:5#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:2:268:5#1/r1.claim: Sukūn on rāʾ elides its dammah before the pronoun suffix, simplifying pronunciation without semantic change.

QIRAAT-ER:2:268:5#2/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:2:268:5#2/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:2:268:5#2/r1.claim: A short dammah, or ishmām, falls between full dammah and sukūn as a canonical articulatory variant.

STUDYQURAN:2:268/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:268/r1.speaker: IK
STUDYQURAN:2:268/r1.claim: IK explains that Satan frightens people with poverty to stop charity and prompts other sins, while God recalls forgiveness and generosity to the soul.

STUDYQURAN:2:268/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:268/r2.speaker: al-Rāzī
STUDYQURAN:2:268/r2.claim: Al-Rāzī says reluctance to give the best can begin with giving only leftovers, then grow into fear of giving any charity.

STUDYQURAN:2:268/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:268/r3.speaker: al-Rāzī
STUDYQURAN:2:268/r3.claim: Al-Rāzī traces miserliness through attachment to all desired things, passive obedience to Satan, abandoning good works, and committing evil.

STUDYQURAN:2:268/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:268/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:2:268/r4.claim: A hadith contrasts Satan’s inspiration to promise evil and lie against truth with an angel’s inspiration to urge good and affirm truth, advising praise of God or refuge from Satan accordingly.

STUDYQURAN:2:268/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:268/r5.speaker: R
STUDYQURAN:2:268/r5.claim: R says Al-Wāsiʿ can mean abundantly generous in forgiveness.
